WASHINGTON, Oct 30 : While dinosaurs ate a lot of different things, including each other, fruit long seemed to have been absent from their menu. But scientists now have found fossils of a turkey-sized and toothless dinosaur possessing a parrot-like head that exhibited multiple adaptations for a specialized fruit diet. This first-known frugivorous dinosaur, named Infernogallus jamesi, lived about 66 million years ago during the Cretaceous Period at the twilight of the age of dinosaurs and displayed traits on its beak and jaws for mashing soft food like fruit. It is known from fossils unearthed in Montana and North Dakota. The name Infernogallus means "hell chicken," a nod to its bird-like appearance and the fact that its fossils were found in the Hell Creek rock formation, which spans the US states of Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota and Wyoming and has yielded the remains of some of the most famous dinosaurs. It would have eaten fruit and other soft plants in the subtropical coastal floodplain ecosystem it shared with the likes of apex predator Tyrannosaurus, three-horned herbivore Triceratops and tank-like armored plant-eater Ankylosaurus.

Infernogallus was about 5 feet (1.5 meters) long and weighed around 25 pounds (11.3 kg). While the fossils — one nearly complete skeleton and isolated bones from a jaw and palate — did not reveal feathers, the researchers believe Infernogallus was covered in them, based on fossils of close relatives. It belonged to a group called theropods that includes T. rex and all the meat-eating dinosaurs, as well as some that took to eating plants and the entire bird lineage. "This definitely expands the range of lifestyles we thought dinosaurs had, and it shows how adaptable theropods were," said paleontologist Greg Funston of Stony Brook University in New York, lead author of the research published in the journal Nature Communications. Fruits are the reproductive structures of angiosperms, also called flowering plants. Angiosperms first appeared earlier in the Cretaceous, around 130 to 140 million years ago, and subsequently took over landscapes previously dominated by plants called gymnosperms like conifers and ginkgoes. Infernogallus shows that some dinosaurs may have had a close ecological relationship with flowering plants. "It has been proposed before that some groups of dinosaurs ate fruits, but there was never evidence to back it up," said study co-author Thomas Dudgeon, a postdoctoral researcher at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto. "The discovery of Infernogallus shows that dinosaur diets were likely far more diverse than we previously thought. Prior to this discovery, there was a bit of a mystery in dinosaur evolution. The evolution of flowering plants introduced a brand-new food source that undoubtedly had consequences for the animals living alongside them," Dudgeon said. The fruit available for Infernogallus may have included various berries as well as drupes, a broad category that today includes types with a central pit like peaches and cherries as well as others like mangoes and olives. THREE KEY FEATURES Infernogallus showed a range of features indicating a frugivorous diet. The three most important, Funston said, were the organization of jaw muscles that powered back-and-forth chewing motions, a mobile joint that enabled the jaw to slide forward, and a series of ridges and grooves on the beak to help mash and shear soft plants like fruits. "We see these features separately in birds and turtles today that eat soft foods, like the fig-eating vulturine parrot or green sea turtles that chew soft sea grass. But no living animal has all three adaptations, showing just how specialized Infernogallus was," Funston said. Infernogallus also shows how adaptable beaks are compared to teeth. "Once you've lost your teeth and developed a beak instead, the range of foods available dramatically increases, including plants, as long as you have some way to digest them," Funston said. Most herbivorous theropods used stomach stones called gastroliths to grind food. But Infernogallus and other members of a lineage called caenagnathids chewed their food instead. Fruit-eating animals play an important role for angiosperms by dispersing seeds. "Mammals and birds would probably also have eaten fruit, but they didn't show the same kinds of specializations for a frugivorous diet that Infernogallus does, so it might have been a less important resource for them. Mammals and birds also were quite small in the Cretaceous, so it's unlikely that they were spreading very large seeds, or that they were spreading them big distances," Funston said. "We know that these big-seeded fruits were proliferating and spreading, and it seems like caenagnathids could have fit this role — although we feel more evidence is needed before drawing that link confidently," Funston said.

SINGAPORE: Hackers stole US$6.3 billion from Binance , the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record digital asset theft. WHAT HAPPENED? About US$6.3 billion of cryptocurrencies were drained from wallets that Binance uses to process transactions, according to the exchange and expert analysis of blockchain records. Binance said in a statement on X that it initially thought the attack involved a compromised laptop.

"However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," it added, without elaborating. The exchange operates a secure asset fund for users, a US$1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customers in the event of a security breach, according to its website.

Co-CEO Richard Teng said losses would be covered by the fund and company resources. According to US blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs, the attackers compromised Binance's "signing infrastructure", which authorises transactions, allowing them to issue instructions that emptied the affected wallets. The bulk of the heist unfolded in about 20 minutes, blockchain records show, beginning shortly after 8pm GMT (4am, Friday, Singapore time) on Thursday (Oct 29). Once the funds were moved, the attackers raced to shift them beyond the reach of Binance counterparties and stablecoin issuers, which have frozen roughly half of the stolen assets. An unusual feature of some cryptocurrencies, including major stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC, is that their issuers can freeze them remotely. "In layman's terms, the attacker may not have stolen the vault key, they may have hijacked the system that tells the vault to release money," said Joshua Chu, a Hong Kong lawyer who works on crypto cases.  WHO IS BEHIND IT?  Several US blockchain analysis firms said the attack bears similarities to previous operations attributed to North Korean hackers. Teng said Binance's investigation had not yet identified the attackers, while North Korea routinely denies involvement in cyberattacks and cryptocurrency thefts. North Korea's mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to requests for comment. TRM said the breach shared characteristics with last year's attack on crypto exchange Bybit, which the FBI attributed to North Korean hackers. The firm said it was highly confident the same group was behind the Binance theft. Chainalysis said funds stolen in an attack last month on Bitget were being mixed with proceeds from the Binance breach.

Related:

Hackers allegedly from North Korea steal US$6.3 billion from Binance in world's biggest crypto heist

WHERE'S THE MONEY? About half the stolen assets were stablecoins that have since been frozen by issuers including Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture. That doesn't mean the coins will be returned to Binance, but it significantly limits the attackers' ability to convert them into cash. TRM said some of the funds had already been posted as collateral to borrow ether and estimated that about US$2.4 billion worth of bitcoin and ether is beyond reach. "No company issues bitcoin or ether and no company can freeze either one," said Patrick Tan, general counsel of ChainArgos, a blockchain intelligence firm in Singapore. "The bitcoin and ether can be stopped only if the attacker sends them to a crypto-asset exchange or broker that is able and willing to freeze them, or if law enforcement obtains the private keys." Market participants said the attackers would likely mix the stolen coins with other assets or use lesser known coins and exchanges to try to move the proceeds. "The more time passes, the less likely they will be able to fold those funds into other exchanges or payment providers — they essentially get blacklisted," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a stablecoin infrastructure company. "In reality a lot of the proceeds of hacks ... (can only be laundered) in the first few hours, but after that happens, you have a lot of different players who know those are marked funds ... and they usually sit there for years." WHAT NEXT? The theft is the latest in a series of major digital asset breaches. Attackers stole US$2.9 billion of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to TRM Labs. The attack has also rattled confidence in the sector. Cryptocurrencies fell on Friday and the total market value of stablecoins declined, suggesting investors were pulling money from digital assets.

Source: Reuters/rj

Oct 30 : Global equity funds saw substantial inflows in the week ended October 28, though at a slower pace, as a rebound in AI and chip stocks, led by South Korea’s SK Hynix after record quarterly profit, lifted demand for technology and Asian funds. Investors bought a net $10.19 billion in global equity funds for a sixth consecutive week of net purchases, though inflows eased from $25.06 billion the previous week, according to LSEG Lipper data. There was, however, some caution in markets over the AI trade ahead of earnings reports from AI hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon. Asian equity funds led regional inflows, attracting $9.9 billion in net purchases, after $11.58 billion the previous week. Investors added $4.54 billion to European funds but withdrew a net $6.65 billion from US equity funds.

Oct 30 : Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance in the world's biggest crypto heist, putting a spotlight on how cryptocurrency exchanges insure their digital assets against theft and cyberattacks. But insurance protection is far from uniform. Coverage depends on how assets are stored, how hackers gain access and the specific terms of the policy. Limited regulation and volatile crypto prices have long made insurers wary of the sector, despite growing demand for protection against digital asset theft and claims against company executives. While both crime and demand for protection have tracked cryptocurrencies' meteoric rise, underwriting such risks remains a niche business offered largely by specialist insurers in the Lloyd's market and in Bermuda.

WHAT IS DIGITAL ASSET INSURANCE? Digital asset insurance is a range of policies designed to protect cryptocurrency exchanges, custodians and other companies operating in the sector against financial losses arising from the theft of digital assets, cyberattacks, technology failures and other business risks. Unlike traditional insurance, these policies are tailored to risks associated with blockchain technology, including the theft or loss of private keys, wallet security breaches, smart contract vulnerabilities and failures in digital asset custody. The global crypto insurance market was valued at $9.37 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $184.98 billion by 2033, according to Data Bridge Market Research. The research firm cited growing institutional adoption of cryptocurrencies and rising incidents of cyberattacks and digital asset theft among the factors driving demand. Coverage can include several types of policies: • Crime insurance for theft, social engineering and scams • Cyber liability for breaches, hacks and regulatory response • Errors and omissions insurance for software bugs, smart contract failures • Directors and officers insurance for lawsuits targeting executives • Technology liability for infrastructure providers HOW ARE LOSSES COVERED? When a crypto exchange suffers a hack, losses can be covered through a combination of insurance payouts, the company's own capital and emergency funds set aside to compensate customers. The extent of insurance coverage depends on the policies held by the exchange, including their limits, deductibles and exclusions. Where losses exceed the insured amount, the company must rely on its own financial resources or other recovery arrangements to meet its obligations. Some exchanges also maintain reserve funds to reimburse customers following security breaches. Binance established the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) in July 2018 as an emergency reserve to protect users in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents. As of 2026, the SAFU fund holds crypto assets worth roughly $1 billion, entirely in bitcoin, according to Binance's website. The company did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment on its insurance coverage. WHAT CAN PREVENT AN INSURANCE PAYOUT? Exclusions that allow insurers to deny certain claims are common in policies covering digital assets as well as the personal liabilities of directors and officers at cryptocurrency companies. These can limit the scope of protection available to companies and make it harder for them to secure coverage. Common exclusions in these policies include value fluctuations, fraudulent acts by the policyholder and unsecured or negligent key management. DO TRADITIONAL CRIME AND CYBER INSURANCE POLICIES COVER CRYPTO? Most standard crime insurance policies do not cover cryptocurrency losses, as they were originally designed to protect physical property such as cash, securities and precious metals. Traditional cyber liability policies also do not always cover the value of digital assets stolen in a hack. While cyber policies can cover both first-party losses and third-party liabilities, including forensic investigations, customer notifications and legal expenses, they generally exclude the loss or transfer of funds. As a result, standalone cyber policies typically do not cover the full value of stolen cryptocurrency unless specific digital asset coverage has been added. HOW DO INSURERS ASSESS CRYPTO THEFT CLAIMS? Insurers examine how a breach occurred, which systems were compromised and whether the resulting loss falls within the policy's coverage. They may also assess whether the exchange followed required security procedures, including controls over private keys, wallet access and transaction approvals. The distinction between an external hacker stealing credentials and an employee deliberately transferring assets can determine whether a crime or cyber insurance policy covers the loss.

MIDTERM VOTE COULD AFFECT AI Tuesday's elections will determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party. Investors are also watching local and state races in Texas and elsewhere on Tuesday for their implications for the data-center buildout. "To the extent that the Democrats really do have a significant blue wave, I think that will be seen as negative for both the AI names, for tech to some extent in general, and maybe even for the market as a whole," said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments. Defense and healthcare are other stock market sectors that could be sensitive to the election results. Any shift in Washington could affect the outlook for fiscal spending that could reverberate through asset prices. Investors were punishing some reports. Along with Alphabet, Caterpillar shares sank 9 per cent on Thursday after the company stuck to its annual sales growth forecast despite strong demand for its power equipment from data centers. "The earnings bar is very high," said Chris Galipeau, head market strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute. "And if you miss or don't jump over that bar, you're in trouble." Apple reports on Monday, with the iPhone maker's shares up 28 per cent so far this year. Results are also expected from semiconductor companies AMD and Qualcomm as well as Palantir, which offers another view of the AI trade. McDonald's, Amgen and ConocoPhillips are among over 100 S&P 500 companies that are due to report next week. Next Friday's employment report for October will give a critical read into the health of the US economy. Data on Thursday showed the US economy in the third quarter grew at its fastest pace in a year, as consumers maintained robust spending and businesses doubled down on investment in AI. The Federal Reserve this week upgraded its assessment of the economy as it held interest rates steady. "I think the missing piece of this strong economic growth narrative is the lack of job growth," said Matthew Miskin, co-chief investment strategist at Manulife John Hancock Investments. As AI and related technology stocks have struggled, other areas of the market have picked up the slack. As October winds down, the energy and financial sectors were set for solid monthly gains, as were defensive groups such as utilities and healthcare. The S&P 500 was last up about 1 per cent for October and over 12 per cent on the year.  "The market is much more broad than people generally want to give it credit for," Galipeau said.

NEW YORK, Oct 30 : US airlines are turning to artificial intelligence to help maximize revenue from airfares. Now startups are putting AI to work on the other side of the transaction, helping passengers automatically claw back savings when ticket prices fall. Companies including JetBack, Junova and Refare monitor fares after customers have booked and seek refunds or flight credits when prices drop. Their pitch is simple: airlines have spent decades building sophisticated pricing systems, while travelers have largely been left to check the prices themselves. The services are emerging as airlines face scrutiny over how they use AI in pricing. While AI's role in aviation continues to evolve, airlines are using the technology to monitor competitors' fares while testing applications aimed at optimizing pricing and improving flight operations. The use of AI has garnered questions from lawmakers over whether the technology could harm consumers if it is used to set individualized pricing based on consumer data and behavior. For travelers, the startups are exploiting a change that followed the COVID-19 pandemic, when many US airlines eliminated change fees on most non-refundable tickets as travelers grew hesitant to book travel amid testing requirements, quarantine rules and border closures. That means a passenger who buys a ticket for $500 may be able to claim the difference if the fare later falls to $400, without additional charges, though airline policies vary.

"AI doesn't have to be a one-sided advantage." Junova said that among 10,000 flights it monitored from September 2025 through July 2026, about 22 per cent experienced at least one fare drop. About 40 per cent of those saw prices decline more than once, illustrating how rapidly fares can change after a passenger has booked. Airfares fluctuate like stock market prices, said AJ Brustein, Junova's co-founder. "They go up and down, often up. But when it goes down, you have an opportunity to get that difference in price back." Junova and Refare charge customers only when they recover money, taking 20 per cent and 25 per cent, respectively, of the savings, while JetBack charges $100 a year. AIRLINES CAN CHANGE THE RULES The business model, however, depends heavily on airlines continuing to accommodate fare drops without imposing large penalties. The COVID-19 crisis weakened a revenue stream for US air carriers, which collected $2.84 billion in reservation cancellation or change fees in 2019. Before the pandemic, change fees on many non-refundable tickets made recovering a modest fare decline impractical. The widespread elimination of those fees created an opening for companies that can continuously monitor prices and pursue credits on customers' behalf. That opening could close. In early October, Alaska Airlines stopped honoring fare drops through customer service, instead directing travelers seeking to capture a lower fare to cancel and rebook under the applicable fare rules. Alaska said it does not charge cancellation fees for its main and first-class fares. But its basic economy tickets are eligible for a credit of 50 per cent of the ticket value when canceled at least 14 days prior to departure. "We're fearful that we could be shut out if other airlines go that route," said Justin Dombrow, founder of Refare. Airlines may nevertheless have reason to tolerate the services. Many fare adjustments on non-refundable tickets are issued as credits rather than cash, requiring passengers to spend the money with the same carrier. "Depending on how you look at it, the refunds are still a win for the airline," Brustein said.

Oct 30 : People who travel across many time zones, like a trip from London to Tokyo, may experience jet lag, with the body's internal 24-hour clock — the circadian rhythm — thrown out of sync with the local time at the arrival location. A new study shows that birds that fly long distances may experience a similar phenomenon that causes them to drift off course. Research involving seabirds called Manx shearwaters found that crossing the Atlantic at speed can throw their internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing errors in the strategy they use to navigate their way home. Birds can use several cues to find their way, including having the sun serve as a compass. A bird flying south sees the sun on its left at sunrise and on its right toward sunset, so it must keep adjusting its heading as the sun moves across the sky. "Animals use an internal clock to do this, the same one that tells our bodies when to sleep, when to be active," said Patrick Lewin, a researcher at the University of Oxford's Department of Biology and one of the leaders of the study published in the journal Science.

To investigate how the birds navigate across vast stretches of open ocean, researchers analysed 20 years of GPS data from 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters, birds that can travel as far as about 1,000 km (620 miles) west from colonies on islands off Britain on foraging trips. Using the positions of the birds and the sun's movement across the sky, the researchers calculated the error each bird should make if its internal clock stayed set to the time at dawn. Across 335 homing flights made out of sight of land, the headings of the birds closely matched those predicted errors.  "The process behind what we're observing here — the mismatch between the internal clock and external time caused by longitudinal movements — is exactly the same as what causes jet lag in humans," Lewin said.  The researchers have not yet investigated whether the clock mismatch affects the birds beyond navigation. But internal clocks influence behaviours including feeding and rest, raising the possibility that those too could be mistimed.  Shearwaters tend to hunt shortly after dawn and before dusk, when fish and other prey are closer to the surface, meaning a mistimed rest period could cost them a feeding opportunity, Lewin said. The study also showed that birds kept using their solar compass even when another source of information was readily available. Along coastlines, where familiar land could potentially guide them, their distance from shore still shifted in the direction predicted by clock-related sun-compass errors. A TWO-STEP PROCESS "For most navigational tasks, it is thought that compass systems are used in conjunction with a map system in a kind of two-step process. In the map step, the animal determines where it is in relation to a goal, such as a home colony. Then in the compass step it uses a compass to translate that into movement," said Tim Guilford, a University of Oxford professor of animal behaviour who was one of the study leaders. The birds may continue to combine these systems even in familiar areas, rather than relying entirely on one or the other.  "If this only produces small deviations, there might not be strong selection against it," Lewin said. Another possibility is that the sun compass helps the birds determine which way to go along the linear feature, Lewin said. Even clouds may not render the sun compass useless. Evidence suggests that birds can sense polarised light and estimate the sun's position unless conditions are heavily overcast, Lewin said. In people, jet lag can cause unpleasant short-term effects and has been linked to longer-term health problems in those who experience it frequently, such as airline pilots and flight attendants. It is not yet known whether birds experience similar effects, but species such as shearwaters that regularly travel rapidly east-west may have evolved ways to cope with repeated disruption to their internal clocks, Lewin said. "Knowing this phenomenon is occurring is only the first step, but perhaps these birds could teach us something about how to treat or avoid jet lag," Lewin said.

TAIPEI, Oct 30 : Foxconn, the world's biggest contract electronics manufacturer, on Friday flagged that a collaboration with leading US artificial intelligence developer OpenAI was in the works, though details were scant. Foxconn Chairman Young Liu told reporters at the company's annual event to showcase its technology that he had met OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman earlier in the day and there would be an announcement once details were confirmed. Liu did not elaborate further. Any deal would build upon last year's agreement between the two firms to work together on designing and engineering data-centre racks, components and other AI hardware. Foxconn, formally called Hon Hai Precision Industry and Nvidia's biggest AI server maker, is increasingly relying on AI infrastructure for growth.

HUMANOID ROBOTS WORKING IN HOUSTON Separately, Foxconn is making progress on plans to deploy humanoid robots at its Houston plant. Brand Cheng, chairman of unit Foxconn Industrial Internet (FII), told Reuters on Friday that more than 10 humanoid robots had been deployed at its Texas facilities for internal use. Foxconn plans to extend deployment beyond Texas, he added. According to presentation materials seen by Reuters, FII introduced two wheeled models in October — one that lifts things vertically and one that can bend at the waist for assembly as well as loading and unloading tasks.
